title: Americans Who Go to Church and Trust Science Are Also More Likely to Believe in Ghosts and Curses - Nautilus
gist: A Social Forces study of the 2025 Baylor Religion Survey (1,812 US adults) finds that people who trust science over church teaching but keep some tie to religion are about twice as likely to believe in magic (ghosts, curses). The finding challenges the assumption that secularization displaces supernatural belief.

insights.claim: Among Americans who believe in God, those scoring high on secular rationalism were about twice as likely to lean toward belief in magic as those who reject it (40% vs. 19%).
insights.speaker: Ruiqian Li
insights.so_what: Trust in science does not crowd out supernatural belief among the religiously attached.

insights.claim: Among people who attend religious services, secular rationalism was linked to magic belief at 28% vs. 19% for non-rationalists, but among those who never attend or do not believe in God the link disappears.
insights.speaker: Ruiqian Li
insights.so_what: The effect requires some residual religious tie, which bounds how far it generalizes.

insights.claim: Magic fits people who still believe in God but no longer let institutions define the supernatural, because it needs no congregation, clergy or theology.
insights.speaker: Ruiqian Li
insights.so_what: Institutional distrust can feed demand for individualized spirituality products.
insights.quote: The magician has a clientele, not a church.
insights.locator: Why are we seeing this trend?

insights.claim: The data is cross-sectional, so it cannot show whether these respondents are drifting from religion, returning to it, or staying put; panel data would be needed.
insights.speaker: Ruiqian Li
insights.so_what: Treat the causal story as unproven.

insights.claim: About 3 in 10 US adults claim no religious affiliation, yet only 5% call themselves atheists and two-thirds of the 'nothing in particular' group still believe in something beyond the natural world.
insights.speaker: Ruiqian Li
insights.so_what: The religiously unaffiliated remain a pool of spiritual demand such as tarot, astrology and psychic services.

insights.claim: The authors suggest younger Americans, who distrust institutions most, are likely to hold both magic and secular rationalist beliefs.
insights.speaker: Ruiqian Li
insights.so_what: Youth-oriented spirituality and wellness offerings may have a durable audience.
insights.locator: It may also explain its appeal to younger Americans
